entries: Ship Engineers operate and maintain main and auxiliary engines, shafting, and generating equipment in engine rooms. They monitor oil temperature, water pressure, and operating parameters to keep propulsion systems stable and safe throughout each voyage.
Monitor operating parameters and alarms for main engines, generators, and boilers.
Switch and replenish fuel, lubricating-oil, and cooling-water systems.
Disassemble and inspect pumps, valves, and turbochargers on schedule and replace seals.
Handle mechanical or electrical failures that occur during voyages.
Complete engine-room logs and maintenance records and assist with port inspections.
Manage spare-parts inventory and energy efficiency and implement pollution-prevention requirements.

paragraphs: Descend into the roaring engine room for shift handoff, first scanning instrument panels and alarm pages. Replenish main-engine oil and clean filters in the morning, then troubleshoot a noisy pump in the afternoon. In the evening, complete the engine-room log and calculate fuel consumption. During night passages, inspect the engine room every two hours, pressing an ear to pipelines for abnormalities, with the smell of engine oil and sea air always on your clothes.

In one sentence: keep the ship powered. The work includes monitoring equipment, replenishing systems, disassembly and maintenance, troubleshooting, recordkeeping, and energy-efficiency management. It requires both tools and engineering judgment, making ship engineers the vessel's propulsion stewards.
